back: Hide ~15% of tokens and predict them from both sides. Loss: mean cross-entropy over the selected positions only.
Of the selected tokens: 80% become the mask, 10% a random token, 10% stay unchanged. All are in the loss.

front: Why not always use the mask token?
back: The mask never appears at inference. Random and unchanged tokens force good representations at every position.
$\log V$ for a vocabulary of $V$ tokens: a sanity check for the initial loss.
Say whether two sentences are consecutive in the corpus or independent (next-sentence prediction). Often dropped later.
Same linear layer on each token vector: $(B,T,d)\to(B,T,K)$.
Start and end vectors give two score arrays $(B,T)$; the answer is the best span $i\le j$ of the passage.
Load pre-trained encoder, add a head, train on a small labelled set with a small learning rate.

front: Why is BERT poor for translation?
back: It is an encoder: it has no decoder to write output text (CNAM deck, p.21).
Encoder-decoder pre-trained to reconstruct the original text from a corrupted version.
Replace spans by sentinels in the input; the target is each sentinel followed by its span, plus a closing sentinel.
Every task is string in, string out, with a task prefix: one model and loss for many tasks.
Causal mask; $-\frac1T\sum_i\log p(x_i\mid x_{<i})$; a training signal at every position.
Encoder: classification, tagging, extractive QA, embeddings. Decoder: free generation, few-shot. Encoder-decoder: translation, summarisation, rewriting.
